summary: Defines two EAP extended key usage values and a certificate extension that carries wireless LAN SSIDs. These let certificates be limited to use in authentication for PPP and wireless networks. It was replaced by RFC 4334.

eli5.summary: A digital ID card can say what it is allowed for. This adds marks saying it is good for Wi-Fi and for dial-up logins.

questions: what are eap extended key usage values
how do certificates list wifi networks
subtitle: Marking certificates as safe for wireless and dial-up authentication.

tldr.problem: When using digital certificates for network authentication via PPP or Wi-Fi, systems need to know which certificate is intended for which network. Without this information, certificate selection is manual and error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two new marks that can be added to certificates to indicate they are safe for use with EAP over PPP or EAP over Wi-Fi (EAPOL). It also adds a certificate extension listing Wi-Fi network names (SSIDs) a certificate is authorized for.
tldr.outcome: Certificate managers and authentication systems can automatically select the right certificate for the current network without user input. It was replaced by RFC 4334, which supersedes this specification.

today: RFC 3770 is obsoleted by RFC 4334, which updates the certificate extension definitions. The extended key usage values and SSID extension remain useful in certificate-based authentication systems for PPP and Wi-Fi networks.

sections.title: Certificate Markup for Authentication Networks
sections.content:
RFC 3770 solves the problem of automatic certificate selection in two network authentication scenarios. When users dial up via PPP or connect to a Wi-Fi network, they present a digital certificate to prove their identity. Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is the authentication method, used both over PPP (dial-up and VPN) and over IEEE 802.1X (Wi-Fi and wired networks).

The RFC defines how to add marks to a certificate to indicate its intended use: either EAP over PPP, or EAP over LAN (EAPOL for Wi-Fi). These marks, called extended key usage values, let a client device automatically select the correct certificate without asking the user.
sections.eli5: When you connect to Wi-Fi or dial up, your computer needs to prove who you are with a certificate. These marks on the certificate tell the computer what it is good for.

sections.title: Extended Key Usage Values
sections.content:
X.509 certificates already support an extended key usage extension that lists the purposes a certificate is valid for (such as signing email or validating server identity). RFC 3770 adds two new purposes: id-kp-eapOverPPP (OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.13) for dial-up and id-kp-eapOverLAN (OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.14) for Wi-Fi.

The certificate issuer decides whether these marks are critical or non-critical. If critical, the certificate MUST only be used for those purposes. If non-critical, the marks serve as hints for automatic selection.
sections.eli5: A certificate can say I am for Wi-Fi or I am for dial-up, or both. The computer uses these labels to pick the right certificate automatically.

sections.title: Wi-Fi Network Name Extension
sections.content:
The RFC also defines a new WLAN SSID certificate extension (OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.1.13) that carries a list of wireless network names (SSIDs) the certificate is authorized for. Each SSID is an octet string of 1 to 32 bytes.

This extension is always non-critical, meaning a system that does not understand it can still process the certificate. The list helps clients pick the right certificate when multiple certificates with Wi-Fi permissions are available.

An attribute certificate can carry the same list as an alternative to a public key certificate extension. Attribute certificates are sometimes used to add information to an existing public key certificate without changing it.
sections.eli5: A certificate can carry a list of Wi-Fi network names it can connect to. When you move between different networks, the device picks the certificate that lists that network.

sections.title: Risks and Privacy
sections.content:
A certificate that lists multiple SSIDs discloses which networks its owner uses, which could be sensitive information. However, the RFC notes that SSIDs are often already visible in Wi-Fi beacon frames and management messages, so adding them to a certificate does not make privacy worse in practice.

A greater risk is incorrect assignment of these marks by the certificate issuer. If a CA mistakenly marks a certificate as valid for a network it should not access, a relying party might accept it. Conversely, if the marks are too restrictive, a legitimate certificate might be rejected.

SSIDs are unmanaged, meaning the same SSID can appear in different networks. If a certificate lists a duplicate SSID, automatic selection fails, and the system should ask the user to choose, or try each certificate until one succeeds.
sections.eli5: If your certificate lists the networks you use, someone watching Wi-Fi traffic might figure out which networks you go to. Also, if the certificate issuer makes a mistake and marks a certificate wrong, the computer might accept or reject it incorrectly.
